### 2026-10-22 – # Did most of the schematic stuff

**3h**

# Did most of the schematic stuff
I'm aware wednesday is a _bit_ late to start your project but whatever. Today i chose some components and almost finished everything necessary for the schematic.

first i decided on my parts (which im still not 100% sure about)  for like 50 minutes

then i worked on the symbol schematic for the board im using. I'm using this one (the lilygo T7-S3, if you were wondering) because I had it lying around at home (it is pretty good), so i dont have to spend nearly half my budget on the board.

![entry1pic4](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/a5e16793e4a41e3703ae865c9968fcbba6f046967601eafafe9df76f5264009b.png)
_this took so loooooooong (prob like 25-ish min but it felt like longer...)_

40 PINS and im probably not even going to use more than like 7

anyways, instead, i get to spend half my budget on the distance sensor! Yay! we love expensive components!

![entry1pic6](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/62a6bafcc6ffb546da39260be19d1b8a4fa62d6e9871c007ec33935e341cda80.png)

i then worked on the  symbol for it, which took me like 15 min of looking at the datasheet

i then realised that this was an I2C only thingy (thankfully before i started the schematic). i looked for my chip's i2C pins...

but i couldnt find them (i dont think it has any). The chip did however, advertise "a STEMMA QT / Qwiic JST-SH connector for easy I2C expansion," , meaning that it was compatible with I2C. after a little digging, i found out that i (might) need one of these connectors:

this is a little weird because this is one of those things meant for prototyping (i think) so its a little weird to be using this with a pcb but _i cant find any I2C pins_

after this i started on the schematic and, since this was a pretty simple one, i finished it (almost) pretty easily

### 2026-10-24 – # Did... A LOT of stuff

**5h**

# Did... A LOT of stuff

First, i found out that  on esp-32's (like the one im using), you can configure the i2c pins, which means no more weird connectors!

 with that done, i moved on to the speaker and amp i'm using. I was initially thinking on using an analog amp, but my chip has 0 DAC(digital analog converters) for output, so i had to use an I2S accepting amp. I then spent an hour learning about I2s and trying to see if my chip supported it (it did):

![entry2pic1](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/503504f358a4784f63c51c1ff3851c2b1da1a10c86992e34b1f1847e2507f4b1.png)

so that was done. with this info in hand i then tried to finish the schematic.

but first! i needed to do the symbol for the amp

![entry2pic7](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/cbad5fe3c012957c8500161de3c8cd049d35f4e4aacdb63a452c281602aba613.png)
this didnt take long at all - like 10 min

i then finished my schematic:
![entry2pic2](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/8e43da2763c8202b1db5a4a24d0abd11c5b2164af240a103de92cccb98a319a5.png)
(the reason the speaker isnt on this is that it's wired directly to the amp and so doesnt need to be on the pcb)

with the schematic done, i moved on to the footprints:

### 2026-10-25 – # Finished the project!

**3.5h**

# Finished the project!

Today I
- wrote a footprint for the amp
- routed the board
- finished(-ish?) a draft of the code

First, i worked on the amp, which was very nice because it HAD GOOD DOCUMENTATION YAYY:

![entry3pic1](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/f3c88de45ccdca5d63c6e9f340caaa289e1a7587da63a00e9ac78880802f322e.png)

one thing that  was a little weird was the vertical spacing of the pins at the bottom, because the diagram gave a value which felt inaccurate,but i figured i could go with it and just bend the headers if it was off:

![entry3pic2](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/4aa5fadd8ba61f9ba776afe08376f5313911d6705c5922bd4e83df714586e031.png)

Then, I routed the board. This was pretty straightforward, and apart from realizing i had misnumbered some of the pads on my lilygo microcontroller, everything was fine, so i finished it in 20 min, and spent the next 25 trying to clean up traces:

![entry3pic5](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/adf3a3e753701f037446efb420dc958c6e02c149fc4386a273db48b157369d37.png)
Then, I started on the code. The distance sensor bit was pretty simple, thanks to the fact that adafruit kindly provided libraries to use with it

![entry3pic7](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/022fb995fba0314e451824f348f14d2125cd02567cda5ede8164d64b966dd3f3.png)

i then moved on to the audio, which took me a while, because there were 4 libraries and I did not know how to use any of them, so I was repeatedly ctrl-tabbing between docs pages and my code. I eventually figured it out after looking at several explanations and segments of example code:

![entry3pic8](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/8ea5dd3db541b2eca3ddeda5e5b9f18cb4d8ff19733ff2fbac1b6b0bea448cfb.png)

and then i did the vibrato feature by using a sine wave that centered around the value to be played:

![entry3pic9](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Txtz56AlpXYSvJEhT04HAEIaAgIKQaYV/e008d24a1d8170054588c5211c025ccc669c7867ae496e1c67a906b99b7a64d8.png)

_the  amplitude is all caps (const), but that's cuz it was initally a constant and then i changed it and was too lazy to go through the code and change it everywhere _
